desc:
You have exactly k identical painted strips, and every strip has the same length L. A strip placed with its left end at position x covers all positions from x to x + L, inclusive; strips may overlap and may be placed anywhere. All the positions listed in points must be covered by at least one strip.

Return the smallest non-negative integer L for which this is possible. (You are allowed to leave strips unused.)

points = [1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 20], k = 2  ->  9

With L = 9, one strip covers 1 to 10 and the other covers 11 to 20. A shorter length would need a strip covering two far apart groups.
hints: If someone told you the length L, how would you count the strips needed? (Think of the leftmost uncovered point.)
Making L larger never needs more strips. So the answer has a monotone yes/no structure that you can search.
Binary search L between 0 and max(points) - min(points). For each candidate L run the greedy: open a strip at the first uncovered point, skip everything within L, count strips, compare with k.
editorial: For a fixed L the minimum number of strips is found greedily: sort the points, put a strip's left end at the first uncovered point and skip all points within L of it. The count is non-increasing in L, so the predicate "L strips suffice with at most k strips" is monotone and we can binary search the smallest L that makes it true.

The upper bound max - min always works with one strip, and 0 works only when there are at most k distinct positions. The search needs about 30 iterations (coordinates up to 109), each a linear scan of the sorted points: O(n log n + n log C) time where C is the coordinate range, O(n) space. An empty list needs no strips, so the answer is 0.
time: O(n log n + n log C)
